text.content:
Cainite justice has a well-earned reputation for being swift and draconian. The Traditions are the fundamental laws of the Camarilla; every other rule or ordinance is an elaboration on those six. Most vampires see the prince and the justicars as the twin faces of justice — the prince locally, the justicars sect-wide — but sheriffs, primogen, archons, and the Inner Circle all shape how the rules are actually applied.

Princely Justice

Within her own domain the prince hears charges and passes judgment, often after the sheriff brings in a suspect. If the accused has evaded capture, or has fled the city, the prince may pass judgment in absentia. Trials vary hugely by prince's temperament — some hold public hearings where accuser and accused may call witnesses or advocates, others allow only the prince to ask questions. If the verdict is guilty and the sentence is destruction, the prince may call a blood hunt. If the primogen disagree strongly enough with a verdict, they may attempt to reverse it by collectively pledging temporary Status equal to the prince's permanent Status (see Status); failure costs each primogen member an additional Status Trait.

Crimes by Tradition

  • The Masquerade: covers anything that could reveal vampires (or other supernaturals) to mortals, including leaving evidence, obvious supernatural displays, or simply spreading information about Kindred existence.
  • Domain: the broadest and most abused charge, since the whole city is the prince's domain — interfering with the sheriff's patrol, the seneschal's papers, or another Kindred's turf can all be framed as violations.
  • Progeny: siring a childe without the prince's permission; some princes extend this to unauthorized ghouling as well.
  • Accounting: used to punish a sire alongside an unwise or poorly-taught childe, or to catch sires who might otherwise dodge a Progeny charge.
  • Hospitality: failing to present oneself to the prince promptly upon entering her city; ignorance of etiquette is no defense.
  • Destruction: killing another (acknowledged, Camarilla) Kindred without the prince's sanction, and diablerie, which almost always draws the harshest possible penalty.

Punishments (roughly descending severity)

  • Final Death — beheading, burning, or other means allowing no return; the default for diablerie and Masquerade breaches.
  • Death/torpor — forced into torpor via blood loss or injury.
  • Long-term staking — staked through the heart and hidden or displayed.
  • Draining and exile — nearly drained of vitae, then driven out.
  • Exile — driven from the city.
  • Blood bonding — forced to drink another Kindred's vitae over three nights, usually binding the criminal to the prince, a primogen, or the victim.
  • Enforced servitude — made to serve another Kindred (even a ghoul).
  • Torture — physical, psychological, or social.
  • Draught of blood — drinks a Kindred's vitae once or twice, edging toward (or completing) a blood bond.
  • Loss of station — stripped of office and its Status/perquisites.
  • Loss of property — deprived of a possession, up to and including the destruction of a childe or ghoul.

The Blood Hunt

Called the Lextalionis by older Cainites, the blood hunt is the Sixth Tradition given teeth: at the prince's command, every Kindred in her domain is authorized to destroy the named quarry and forbidden to aid him. A prince may leave participation optional or demand it outright, sometimes offering a reward (the quarry's possessions, a Status Trait, even the office of the sheriff who let the quarry slip). Tradition holds that whoever brings down the quarry has tacit permission to diablerize him unless the prince expressly forbids it.

The Hue and Cry

Only the prince may declare a blood hunt; anyone else invoking the Lextalionis (even nominally in the prince's name) has committed a Domain violation and can expect the prince's wrath along with anyone who joined that unauthorized hunt. How avidly the city pursues the hunt tracks popular sentiment: Kindred hunt eagerly against diablerists, mass-murderers of other Kindred, Masquerade-breakers, or Sabbat collaborators, but grow suspicious of a prince who calls hunts over mere political inconvenience.

Rules of the Hunt

  • No one may aid the fugitive or interfere with the hunters; helping the quarry is itself treated as a crime.
  • The Masquerade must not become a casualty of the hunt — bringing down the criminal is worthless if a bigger secret gets exposed doing it.
  • The hunt ends at the city limits as a rule of thumb, not a hard law; hunters who chase the quarry into another prince's domain risk that prince's wrath.
  • The hunt does not end until the quarry is destroyed — even if the prince who called it dies, new evidence exonerates the quarry, or the quarry flees to another city, the hunt (and the quarry's marked name) persists until proof of death is delivered.

Princes may add their own rules on top of these (e.g., barring diablerie, or restricting the hunt to a particular clan in a particular area), and it is every Kindred's responsibility to know any such addenda. Hunters may use Influence Traits (Police, Street, Transportation, Underworld, Media, and others) to track or hem in the quarry; a Narrator may allow a character to reach into an Influence area she doesn't formally hold by requiring one extra Trait spent versus someone who does. A cornered quarry typically has three options: run, distract (often by breaching the Masquerade himself, which can make him unwelcome even in a city willing to shelter him from the original hunt), or make a stand on ground of his choosing. A blood hunt quarry who is forced to return to the hunting city later must tread carefully — there is no formal pardon in Cainite law, and old allies may have drifted away.

Archons

Archons are the eyes and ears of the Camarilla's six justicars (one per founding clan), sent to investigate rumors of anarch or Sabbat collusion, repeated Masquerade failures, or a prince subverting the Traditions. An archon operating in an official capacity receives two additional Status Traits, Empowered and Feared, which cannot be permanently lost while she holds the position. She may strip a permanent Status Trait (at no cost to herself) from any Kindred who hinders her investigation or sentence — reversible only by a justicar — and may detain, interrogate, or destroy any Kindred, though she must later justify her actions to her justicar. If she can provide good reason, an archon is exempt from the Sixth Tradition. Archons typically work either as moles (entering quietly under a false identity, tacitly excused from the Fifth Tradition by the justicars) or as showmen (announcing themselves with overt authority and a list of demands, sometimes to pressure a guilty party into a mistake, sometimes to mask which of several suspects is truly being hunted).

The Red List and Anathema

Vampires whose infamy or treachery has earned the hatred of the entire Camarilla are called Anathema, and their names and crimes are recorded on the Red List kept in the halls of Elysium everywhere. Anyone on the Red List is subject to a standing, permanent blood hunt across all Camarilla territory. Mere Sabbat membership, diablerie, or infernalism is not, by itself, enough — only acts monstrous even by vampiric standards merit the Red List. Two justicars must agree the crimes are heinous enough to call a conclave on the matter; at that conclave the justicars present their evidence, and unless a compelling defense is raised, the accused is added to the list. The only way off the Red List is death.

Alastors

Alastors are the secret enforcers of the Inner Circle, devoted chiefly to hunting the Anathema. Most are recruited quietly from among the most capable archons; the rare exception is any vampire who destroys an Anathema on her own initiative, who is recruited immediately. An alastor gains two additional Status Traits, Sanctioned and Feared, unlosable short of being declared Anathema herself; she may strip a permanent Status Trait at no cost from anyone hindering her mission, and is immune to prosecution on any scale below a conclave. A vampire who destroys an Anathema is granted the prey's possessions, entry into the alastors, and the Trophy (also called the Mark of the Beast) — a thaumaturgically-applied tattoo on the right palm, detectable even through gloves by those in the know, that signals to other officials she should not be mistaken for a threat. Alastors are forbidden to diablerize their prey; breaking that rule (or defecting from the Camarilla) marks the alastor herself for destruction. The most accomplished alastors, those who've destroyed one of the five highest-ranked Anathema, are called Red Alastors and are rumored to hold even greater authority.

Conclaves

A conclave is a grand assembly of Kindred called when a situation exceeds the resources of a single city. There are three recognized types: grand conclaves (huge, international, called for truly momentous events), regional conclaves (concerning several cities or part of a continent), and judicial conclaves (trials for Kindred whose age or power places them beyond princely justice). Only a justicar may call a conclave (a prince with an unusually strong reputation might get away with requesting one through her local archon, but this is rare and risky).

Setting Up

The justicar selects the host city, often deliberately away from the epicenter of the problem, and gives the host prince four to eight weeks' notice (less for urgent matters); declining the honor is technically allowed but marks a prince as suspect. The justicar names whoever is in charge of conclave security (an existing archon, or a Kindred who thereby gains archon-equivalent rank and privileges for the duration). Hosting a conclave costs the prince and her staff enormously in preparation: security against Sabbat/anarch action, housing and feeding hundreds of guests, and quietly cleaning up embarrassments before outsiders arrive. Word invariably leaks locally within about a week, though official notice to the wider Camarilla goes out roughly a month before the event. Any Camarilla vampire who hears of a conclave concerning a matter of interest to her may attend; independents are occasionally permitted but closely watched, and the Sabbat are far more often a conclave's topic than its guests.

The Conclave Itself

Proceedings typically open at midnight on the announced night. Seating is by age and power. The presiding justicar addresses the assembly, recognizes speakers, and keeps discussion on track (with the right to limit long-winded speakers or eject disruptive ones) — notably, a conclave is one of the few settings where even a neonate is formally guaranteed the right to be heard, though getting the justicar's attention from the back of the hall is another matter. Business is traditionally capped at eight hours per night. Once the justicar judges the matter thoroughly discussed, he summarizes the leading options, calls a recess for private lobbying, then reconvenes for a vote open to every Kindred present (by show of hands or written ballot, tallied by archons). The justicar then formally declares the result binding on the whole Camarilla. A closing party usually follows, and the justicar departs for the Inner Circle soon after, sometimes leaving an archon or two to ensure a smooth wind-down.

Afterward

Visitors are expected to leave promptly (the sheriff often has to encourage stragglers), and it can take the host city a month or more to fully return to normal. Kindred who hosted or ran security well can expect a Status Trait in reward; those who badly bungled their responsibilities can lose Status commensurate with the size of the conclave and the scale of their failure — up to two Traits for a small conclave, as many as five for the largest.

Judicial Conclaves

Called specifically to try Kindred whose age or power puts them beyond a prince's authority. These are far less social than other conclaves: guilt is effectively assumed going in, and the accused must actively prove her innocence. The presiding justicar (often flanked by archons) keeps discussion narrowly focused on guilt or innocence, and the trial concludes with a vote of all present, though the justicar may overrule the vote if he suspects coercion or serious corruption — in which case he may instead order a trial by ordeal, a demanding, time-limited quest where failure means death. Sentence is carried out immediately after the verdict, and the justicar departs soon after, sometimes leaving an archon behind briefly to protect any witnesses who testified unpopularly.
